title: POC check-in: SIEM export validation (Splunk + Sentinel)
summary: Helio Bank validated Redwood Private audit log export into Splunk HEC and Azure Sentinel. The team confirmed event delivery but found schema consistency issues across event types (missing schema_version on some events, actor fields inconsistent for console vs API actions, missing source_ip in a subset, and duplicates during exporter retries). Redwood walked through schema v1 rollout plan, normalization in the exporter, and recommended SIEM de-dupe strategy using event_id + idempotency_key. Follow-ups were captured and mapped to existing tickets/PRs.
topics: Azure Sentinel / Log Analytics connector behavior
Schema v1 required fields: schema_version, event_id, actor.*, target.*, resource_*
Duplicates due to retry semantics and recommended de-dupe keys
Private parity gaps (RBAC change events + export config changes)
Redaction / PII handling (no secrets, hashed identifiers)
questions: Can we rely on schema_version being present for every event across all producers (console, control plane, installer)?
What is the canonical dedupe key for SIEM when exporter retries cause duplicates?
Will actor.impersonated_by be populated for admin/support sessions, and how do we detect it?
Do you emit before/after summaries for policy and retention changes, and how is cardinality controlled?
action_items: Kevin Osei - Share updated exporter configuration snippets for Splunk HEC + Sentinel, including recommended batching/retry settings - due 2026-02-24
Dana Kim - Send 10 raw sample events showing the missing schema_version + missing source_ip cases (redacted) - due 2026-02-21
Markus Klein - Provide Helio a one-page SIEM field mapping + example Splunk/Sentinel queries (event_id dedupe, actor filters) - due 2026-02-26
Liam O'Rourke - Confirm timeline for Private patch rollout that includes normalization and schema_version tagging - due 2026-02-25
next_steps: Helio to re-run POC validation after exporter normalization build is deployed
Redwood to follow up with written guidance on de-dupe + at-least-once semantics
Schedule 30-min follow-up to review updated samples and confirm acceptance criteria
links_mentioned: Jira SUP-18477 (SIEM export events not normalized)
Jira SUP-18510 (duplicates in SIEM due to retry semantics)
Linear ENG-4836 (Splunk HEC + Azure Sentinel exporter targets)
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-20
Start time: 09:00 PT
Duration: 43 min
Attendees (Redwood): Liam O'Rourke, Markus Klein, Kevin Osei
Attendees (Helio Bank): Dana Kim, Arjun Mehta, Renee Alvarez

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Customer tested audit log export to Splunk HEC and Azure Sentinel.
- Observed schema inconsistencies across event types.
- Observed duplicates during exporter retries.
- Agreed on follow-up: send raw samples, Redwood to share de-dupe and schema guidance.

Transcript

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Hey everyone. Thanks for making the time. This is the POC check-in on SIEM export validation, Splunk and Sentinel. Dana, Arjun, Renee, good to see you.

[00:10] Dana Kim: Yep, hi. We ran the test yesterday and this morning. We have some, uh, findings.

[00:16] Markus Klein: Great. And Kevin is on too, he’s been living in the exporter code, so we should be able to answer the gnarly bits.

[00:23] Kevin Osei: Hey all.

[00:25] Arjun Mehta: Morning. I’ve got logs pulled up, Splunk and also the Log Analytics workspace.

[00:33] Liam O'Rourke: Awesome. Maybe quick agenda: what worked, what didn’t, then define acceptance criteria and next steps. Dana, want to start with what you saw?

[00:44] Dana Kim: Sure. So, good news: we can ingest. Splunk HEC is receiving events, and Sentinel is receiving via the HTTP collector we set up. But we’re seeing inconsistent fields. Like, some events have schema version, some don’t. Some have actor fields in one shape, and others it’s like… different casing or missing.

[01:05] Renee Alvarez: And from a GRC standpoint, we need it to be predictable. Like if we say “audit logs include actor, action, target, time, result,” that has to be consistent.

[01:15] Kevin Osei: Yeah, that aligns with what we’re tightening up with schema v1 and normalization. Can you give an example of the missing schema_version? Which event types?

[01:25] Arjun Mehta: I can paste one. Well, I can’t paste in Zoom chat because policy but I can describe. We have events where event_type is something like rbac.role.update, and it has schema_version = 1.0. But then console export config change events, I think it was audit.export.destination.update, those came through without schema_version.

[01:45] Dana Kim: Also, in the console ones, actor.id is sometimes an email, which we don’t love, and in the API ones it’s a UUID. So we can’t join cleanly.

[01:55] Markus Klein: Got it. For the email: it should be a stable user_id, and we can include actor.display as the email if it’s allowed by your config, but the canonical identifier should not be the email. We’ve been pushing towards “id + type + display”. Kevin, is that in the schema requirement?

[02:10] Kevin Osei: Yep. In v1, actor_type and actor_id are required. actor_display is optional. For PII minimization we prefer actor_display to be either redacted or role-based, but some customers do want it.

[02:24] Dana Kim: We don’t want emails in Splunk by default. We can hash it, but it’s extra.

[02:30] Kevin Osei: Understood. We can make sure the producer doesn’t send email as the id field. If display is present, we can configure redaction/hashing at export too, but primary fix is “don’t put email in actor_id”.

[02:45] Liam O'Rourke: And just to confirm, in your POC config did you enable “include human-readable actor fields” or was it default?

[02:53] Arjun Mehta: Default. We didn’t flip any “verbose” flags.

[02:56] Kevin Osei: Okay, then that’s a bug on our side.

[03:00] Dana Kim: Second issue: duplicates. We’re seeing the same event repeated like two or three times. Not huge volume, but it’s there.

[03:09] Arjun Mehta: Yeah, same timestamp, same payload, different Splunk _time maybe off by a second. Looks like retry.

[03:18] Kevin Osei: That is retry. Exporter is at-least-once, so duplicates are possible during transient failures. We need to ensure event_id is stable and you can de-dupe in the SIEM. Do your duplicates have same event_id or different?

[03:33] Arjun Mehta: That’s the thing: some have event_id, and those match. But some don’t have event_id, so we can’t de-dupe reliably.

[03:43] Dana Kim: Yeah. We basically need a canonical dedupe key.

[03:48] Kevin Osei: Agree. In schema v1, event_id is required. For legacy producers we’re normalizing and generating event_id if missing, but it should be deterministic per event, not per retry attempt. That’s in the normalization work.

[04:03] Markus Klein: The guidance we’ve been giving is: de-dupe on event_id first. If you want extra safety, use (event_id, schema_version). Some customers also use idempotency_key, but that’s more internal.

[04:14] Dana Kim: What about correlation ids? We’d like request id or trace id.

[04:19] Kevin Osei: Yep. request_id and trace_id are being standardized, plus admin_action_id for console workflows that are multi-step. There was a gap where some console actions didn’t propagate request_id all the way to the audit emitter.

[04:34] Renee Alvarez: When you say “admin_action_id,” is that something we can use to reconstruct a sequence? Like approval then change then export?

[04:43] Markus Klein: Exactly. Think of it like a parent id for the human workflow, even if multiple services are involved. Still early but we’re making it consistent.

[04:54] Dana Kim: Another thing: source IP. Some events have source_ip, some don’t. For security review, that’s kind of table stakes.

[05:03] Kevin Osei: Yeah. We have source_ip as required when the action is initiated via an HTTP request and we can reasonably capture it. For async/internal actions, it might be absent, but for console and API it should be present. Missing source_ip is likely another producer inconsistency.

[05:22] Arjun Mehta: For Sentinel, we also saw the fields coming in flattened weird. Like actor.id becomes actor_id in one place but actor.id in another, because the connector is doing its own thing.

[05:34] Kevin Osei: Sentinel tends to flatten nested JSON depending on ingestion path. We can support both flattened and dotted, but the exporter should ideally emit a consistent shape. We decided on top-level stable fields with namespaced extensions to keep SIEM compatibility.

[05:51] Markus Klein: Right, and this is why we are leaning “flattened” for the canonical schema, not deep nested objects. Some of our older producers still emit nested actor: {id:..., type:...}.

[06:03] Dana Kim: I don’t care if it’s flat or nested, I just need it consistent.

[06:08] Liam O'Rourke: Totally fair. For this POC, acceptance criteria is: consistent event fields across event types, and de-dupe strategy works, and you can filter by actor and action reliably.

[06:20] Renee Alvarez: And retention statement. Like, how long are audit logs retained if export fails.

[06:27] Kevin Osei: In Private, by default we buffer locally for 72 hours in the queue, configurable. If export is down longer, you can backfill depending on your storage settings. We have a runbook, but for customer-facing we keep it as “buffering + retry; at-least-once; duplicates possible; no guarantee of exactly-once.”

[06:49] Dana Kim: Okay. The buffer is fine, but we want to be notified if it’s backing up.

[06:54] Markus Klein: We have metrics: export success rate, drop rate, queue depth, delivery latency. For Private, you can scrape them into Prometheus or forward to your monitoring. We can send the dashboard link, but for POC we can at least get you the metric names.

[07:11] Arjun Mehta: On the schema: can you confirm which fields are required in v1? Like list.

[07:18] Kevin Osei: High level: schema_version, event_id, event_type, occurred_at, result (success/failure), tenant_id (or org id), actor_type, actor_id. Then optional: actor_display, source_ip, user_agent, request_id, trace_id, target_* fields, resource_* fields, and diff summary for before/after changes.

[07:43] Dana Kim: We saw diff summary in some events, but it was like huge JSON. That’s going to blow up cardinality.

[07:50] Kevin Osei: Yep. We don’t ship full object diffs. It should be a constrained “fields_changed” list and a before/after snippet that’s allow-listed. If you saw full JSON, that’s a bug or misconfiguration.

[08:06] Markus Klein: Also we can keep diffs as strings like “role_permissions: [added: X, removed: Y]” rather than full structures. That’s the intent.

[08:17] Dana Kim: Good. Another item: RBAC change events in Private. We expected role update events when we changed role membership via the UI. We got some, but not all.

[08:30] Arjun Mehta: Specifically, adding a user to a role produced an event. Removing a user didn’t. Or it might have, but it didn’t show in Splunk.

[08:40] Kevin Osei: That might be the issue from the earlier support ticket. There’s a known gap in one code path. Is this the “remove member” endpoint in the control plane?

[08:51] Markus Klein: We had a report where “PATCH role members” emitted, but “DELETE member” didn’t. That’s being covered under sensitive action coverage, but we should address it here too.

[09:02] Liam O'Rourke: We can tie it to the existing follow-up. I’ll make sure support references it. Do you have exact timestamps when you removed?

[09:10] Arjun Mehta: Yes, around 08:14 UTC.

[09:13] Dana Kim: We can send the raw samples.

[09:16] Kevin Osei: Perfect.

[09:18] Renee Alvarez: And export destination changes—those should definitely be audited. That’s like someone turning off the feed.

[09:25] Markus Klein: Agreed. Export config changes are explicitly sensitive. They should emit audit.export.destination.create/update/delete with actor, previous/new, and scope.

[09:37] Dana Kim: We got the event, but it was missing schema_version and missing source_ip. Which is, ironically, the event you most want source_ip on.

[09:47] Kevin Osei: Yeah. That’s exactly the type we’re normalizing. The exporter PR we have—842—tags schema_version and also normalizes legacy producers to v1 shape. That should fix missing schema_version, and we can fix the source_ip capture in the console backend.

[10:08] Liam O'Rourke: Timeline-wise, Kevin, what’s realistic for Helio? They want to complete POC by end of next week.

[10:15] Kevin Osei: For exporter normalization, we have it in review now. We can get you a Private build early next week, like Tuesday/Wednesday, assuming no surprises.

[10:26] Dana Kim: Okay.

[10:28] Arjun Mehta: For Splunk, can you recommend sourcetype and indexes? We used “redwood:audit” but not sure.

[10:36] Markus Klein: “redwood:audit” is what we’ve used. Index is up to your standard. We also suggest setting HEC ack on, so we can detect ingestion issues and not just fire-and-forget.

[10:49] Kevin Osei: Yep, and with HEC ack, retries can be more frequent if Splunk is slow, which increases duplicates, so de-dupe becomes more important.

[11:00] Dana Kim: That’s fine. We’ll de-dupe if we have event_id.

[11:05] Kevin Osei: Exactly.

[11:08] Renee Alvarez: From documentation side, do you have something we can point to? Like a schema doc.

[11:14] Liam O'Rourke: We have an audit log schema v1 doc we can share, plus a versioning/backcompat policy. For external sharing, we’ll send a customer-safe PDF excerpt, not internal links. Markus can package that.

[11:30] Markus Klein: Yep. I’ll also add example queries: “show failed auth events by source_ip,” “show role changes by actor,” that kind of thing.

[11:42] Dana Kim: Okay. Can we talk about naming? event_type strings are mostly good, but we saw some like “rbac.change” and others “rbac.role.update”. We’d like a stable taxonomy.

[11:53] Kevin Osei: That’s part of the taxonomy registry. Unknown or legacy event types are being mapped to canonical types in normalization. In v1, you should see consistent event_type names.

[12:07] Arjun Mehta: Cool.

[12:09] Dana Kim: One more: we saw actor_type sometimes “apiKey” and sometimes “api_key”. Case matters in Splunk searches.

[12:18] Kevin Osei: Yep, that’s exactly why we made it an enum. It should be “api_key” consistently. Again, normalization can fix older ones.

[12:30] Markus Klein: And if you want, we can provide a field dictionary so you can pre-build dashboards without chasing variations.

[12:38] Dana Kim: That would help.

[12:41] Liam O'Rourke: Okay. Let’s capture issues as: (1) missing schema_version on some console/export config events, (2) missing source_ip on some UI-initiated events, (3) actor_id wrongly being email, (4) inconsistent actor_type casing, (5) duplicates due to retry and missing event_id on some, and (6) RBAC member removal event missing.

[13:05] Dana Kim: That’s the list.

[13:07] Renee Alvarez: Plus the diff payload being too verbose in one case.

[13:12] Kevin Osei: Right. Add (7) diff summary cardinality issue.

[13:17] Arjun Mehta: I’ll send samples for (1), (2), (5), and (7). For RBAC removal, I’ll send the approximate times and the UI steps.

[13:28] Kevin Osei: Great.

[13:30] Liam O'Rourke: Kevin, can you map these to the tickets you’re already tracking? So we don’t lose it.

[13:36] Kevin Osei: Yeah. SUP-18477 is the normalization/field inconsistency. SUP-18510 is duplicates. ENG-4827 is exporter normalization. ENG-4830 is correlation ids. And ENG-4836 covers Splunk/Sentinel targets. The RBAC missing removal is tied to the Private parity work, but we can link to the earlier private missing RBAC events report.

[13:57] Markus Klein: And I’ll put a note in the POC tracker that these are gating for sign-off.

[14:04] Dana Kim: Appreciate it.

[14:06] Liam O'Rourke: Anything else you need from us to complete validation?

[14:10] Dana Kim: Just the written de-dupe guidance, and confirm that schema_version will be present for every event.

[14:17] Kevin Osei: After normalization rollout, yes, every exported event will include schema_version and event_id. For raw internal ingestion, some legacy producers might still emit older shape, but exporter normalizes so what you see in SIEM is consistent.

[14:34] Arjun Mehta: For Sentinel, is there any special mapping? We saw it flattening.

[14:39] Kevin Osei: We’ll provide a recommended table mapping. Also the exporter can emit in a flatter format explicitly for Sentinel if needed, but we’re trying to keep one format.

[14:52] Renee Alvarez: Okay.

[14:54] Liam O'Rourke: Cool. Let’s do next steps: Dana sends raw samples tomorrow. Kevin sends config snippets and confirms build date by Wednesday. Markus sends one-pager queries and field mapping. We’ll meet again end of week?

[15:10] Dana Kim: Thursday works.

[15:12] Arjun Mehta: Yep.

[15:14] Liam O'Rourke: Great, I’ll send an invite for Thursday 9am PT.

[15:18] Markus Klein: Thanks all.

[15:20] Kevin Osei: Thanks.

[15:22] Dana Kim: Thanks.

(Transcript continues with light scheduling/crosstalk; end of recording.)
